radford.name: C. A. Ralegh Radford · official guide, 1974 reprint

teiloChurch.name: Church in Wales · St Teilo, Merthyr Mawr

milestones.title: A landscape with a long memory.
milestones.summary: Merthyr Mawr's sands preserve traces of people long before the Normans: Stone Age flints, Bronze Age burials, Iron Age hearths and Roman material. The castle belongs to one chapter of a much older landscape.
milestones.context: Heneb describes a landscape where shifting sand repeatedly conceals and reveals remains from different periods. Settlement, cultivated land and burials are part of the Warren's buried archaeology. These traces set the scene for the later stories of worship, homes and work in the valley.
milestones.dateNote: This opening chapter brings together prehistoric and Roman evidence; the early Christian memorials are considered next.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · St Teilo's, present-day-inspired study
milestones.title: Before the castles: stones of remembrance.
milestones.summary: Long before either castle, memorial stones suggest an early Christian presence at Merthyr Mawr. Cadw dates some stones from the church site to the fifth and sixth centuries. St Teilo's churchyard preserves this older story beside a much later church.
milestones.context: The collection includes memorial pillars and later carved stones; Church in Wales also records eleventh- and twelfth-century headstones. These are traces of remembrance across several centuries, not the remains of one building. A medieval font, stoup and piscina survive from the church which preceded today's building. Cadw dates the present church to 1849–51, designed by Benjamin Ferrey with interior fittings by John Prichard.
milestones.dateNote: The early dates belong to memorial stones which suggest an early religious site. They do not establish an exact church foundation year or a personal foundation by St Teilo. The illustrated building is Victorian, not a fifth-century church.

milestones.title: A stronghold beside the ford.
milestones.summary: William de Londres establishes a Norman castle beside a crossing of the Ewenny. Earth banks and timber defences come first; an early stone keep follows. William is recorded here by 1116.
milestones.context: The surviving earthworks explain the first castle's shape. The keep is among the region's earliest Norman stone buildings, although its precise building sequence and attribution need care. Ogmore formed part of a wider landscape of castles that also included Coity and Newcastle.
milestones.dateNote: Cadw places the beginnings in the early 12th century. William is recorded at Ogmore by 1116. The stones are probably medieval, but cannot be dated specifically to this earliest phase; their omission here does not prove they were absent.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · present-day-inspired Ewenni Priory study
milestones.title: A priory takes root nearby.
milestones.summary: Maurice de Londres founds Ewenni Priory as a Benedictine offshoot of Gloucester Abbey. The church and its later defensive enclosure become another lasting expression of Norman power in the valley.
milestones.context: A church existed before the establishment of the monastic community. Cadw dates the priory foundation to 1141, while the historic environment record describes an earlier cell. The substantial enclosing walls belong to later development; they should not all be assigned to the foundation year.
milestones.dateNote: 1141 dates the monastic foundation. The surviving church and enclosure also contain later work.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · estimated castle & crossing, c.1250–1300
milestones.title: The castle grows around its keep.
milestones.summary: A stone curtain wall, gateway, bridge and further buildings strengthen the enclosure. The older keep remains at its heart. The inner ditch is designed to take in sea water at high tide.
milestones.context: Cadw's architectural record places this major building phase in the early 13th century. The internal ground was raised and additional steps were needed down to the older cellar. The small castle's surviving banks and ditches still help explain how successive phases fitted together.
milestones.dateNote: The early 13th century is an architectural phase; the precise construction years remain uncertain. The illustrated crossing is a medieval interpretation: its founding year and original arrangement are unknown.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · estimated castle & crossing, c.1250–1300
milestones.title: An inheritance reaches Lancaster.
milestones.summary: Maud de Chaworth's marriage to Henry of Lancaster links Ogmore to a powerful new family. The castle's role increasingly centres on the administration of its lordship, as well as its defences.
milestones.context: The official Radford guide gives 1297 for the marriage; Cadw and Coflein give 1298. The inheritance joins Ogmore to the Lancaster family's estates. Coflein records the castle's later connection with the Crown in 1399, extending that story beyond the family marriage.
milestones.dateNote: The sources differ between 1297 and 1298; the timeline uses the broader period. The illustrated crossing is a medieval interpretation: its founding year and original arrangement are unknown.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · Candleston ruins, present-day-inspired study
milestones.title: A second castle rises beyond the river.
milestones.summary: Beyond the Ewenny, Candleston takes shape as a fortified home for the de Cantilupe family. Its small tower and domestic rooms tell a different story from Ogmore's Norman stronghold: a manor house whose owners combined residence with defence.
milestones.context: The surviving fabric is dated to the early fourteenth century. A hall range was added around 1500, followed by further wings and stables. Sand affected the surrounding settlement, but the house continued in use. Cadw records John Nicholl living here while his new Merthyr Mawr house was built in 1806–09; Coflein records later use as a farmhouse into the late nineteenth century.
milestones.dateNote: The 1300s anchor the earliest surviving masonry, not every wall. The settlement's loss under sand and the house's later abandonment happened on different timescales. The painting is a present-day-inspired ruin study, not a medieval reconstruction.

milestones.title: The valley is caught in revolt.
milestones.summary: Ogmore Castle suffers serious damage during the years of Owain Glyndŵr's revolt. The surrounding settlement also contracts. This was a working valley of tenants, meadows and mills, as well as a place of military power.
milestones.context: Coflein's fulling-mill record dates damage at the castle to 1402–05. It cites medieval accounts for a mill near the castle in the 1300s, whose exact position is unknown. Heneb records a sharp fall in the settlement's tenants after the rebellion: a glimpse of the upheaval beyond the walls.
milestones.dateNote: The dated evidence describes castle damage during the revolt. This scene imagines the aftermath; individual damaged walls and roofs are speculative. The crossing's founding year and medieval arrangement are unknown.

milestones.title: A stronghold becomes a ruin.
milestones.summary: Ogmore's main castle buildings fall out of use between the 1530s and 1631. Yet the site does not simply disappear from local life: the courthouse continues its work among the changing buildings.
milestones.context: Coflein gives a broad abandonment interval for the main castle, rather than a single day when every room was deserted. The courthouse's longer use shows how administration could continue after the fortress's main buildings had fallen out of use. Candleston's separate history belongs to the fortified-home chapter.
milestones.dateNote: The 1530s–1631 interval concerns Ogmore's main castle buildings, not the end of all activity at the site.

milestones.title: Justice among the ruins.
milestones.summary: Long after the castle's military life has faded, its courthouse remains in use. Coflein records court activity continuing into 1803: a reminder that a ruined fortress could still be part of everyday administration.
milestones.context: The courthouse stood in the outer bailey. Its long administrative life keeps the castle site connected to local affairs even as other buildings decay. The record of continued use into 1803 provides a late glimpse of that enduring role.
milestones.dateNote: 1803 anchors continued use; the date of a final hearing is uncertain.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · Merthyr Mawr landscape study
milestones.title: A new estate shapes the valley.
milestones.summary: Merthyr Mawr House is built for Sir John Nicholl. The landscape park develops around it through the early 19th century, adding another layer to the valley's paths, gardens, woodland and agricultural setting.
milestones.context: Cadw dates the house to 1806–09 and describes the park's design and planting between 1806 and 1838, much of it after completion of the house. The registered landscape also preserves evidence of an earlier estate, bringing several centuries of land use together in the wider valley.
milestones.dateNote: House-building dates are distinguished from the longer creation of the park.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · present-day-inspired Warren landscape study
milestones.title: Rifle practice among the dunes.
milestones.summary: The Warren also held a place for target practice. RCAHMW identifies a volunteer rifle range west of Candleston on an Ordnance Survey map dated 1877, adding a military-training chapter to this changing landscape.
milestones.context: The map shows an 800-yard range running roughly north-north-east to south-south-west, with targets at the north end. RCAHMW notes that some mapped firing points fall behind high dunes, so their practical use is uncertain. The range is absent from the 1899 map; the record suggests a later replacement farther west.
milestones.dateNote: 1877 dates the map evidence, not the range's opening. The reviewed records do not securely identify the volunteer unit. The painting is a landscape study, not a reconstruction of the range.

milestones.title: A future for the ruins.
milestones.summary: The castle enters guardianship, securing public access and responsibility for its care. A Welsh Government record confirms the exact date. Today management and maintenance responsibilities rest with Welsh Ministers through Cadw.
milestones.context: The 2023 government response identifies a guardianship agreement beginning on 1 August 1928. The arrangement secures management, maintenance and public access. It continues in perpetuity, with care responsibilities exercised today through Cadw.
milestones.dateNote: An exact date confirmed by the Welsh Government's guardianship record.

milestones.artLabel: AI generated · present-day-inspired dune landscape study
milestones.title: Care reaches beyond the castle.
milestones.summary: NRW's reserve-management lease ends in 2020, returning responsibility to Merthyr Mawr Estate. A new conservation agreement is reported in 2023, bringing the Estate and NRW together in caring for the Warren's habitats.
milestones.context: NRW announced the lease's end on 31 December 2020 and plans for a nature reserve agreement. The Estate's land agent reported the new agreement in July 2023, with direct Estate management and NRW advice and monitoring. Conservation grazing, habitat work and invasive-species control are part of this landscape's recent story.
milestones.dateNote: The lease ended on 31 December 2020; the new agreement was reported on 19 July 2023.

milestones.title: A crossing through the centuries.
milestones.summary: The stones probably began in the medieval period and were altered later. Records also recall baptisms beside the Ewenny and a possible supporting role for Old Star Cottage. This is a story of local life, not a sign that the crossing is safe today.
milestones.context: Cadw describes a crossing of about 35 metres linking the castle bank with the floodplain between the Ewenny and Ogmore. RCAHMW's record of Old Star Cottage, a mid-eighteenth-century home near the stones, notes the area's association with baptisms and suggests the cottage was used during preparations. The reviewed record does not give a date or identify a particular ceremony.
milestones.dateNote: The stones' builder and founding year remain uncertain. The cottage's suggested baptism role is qualified, and no date or denomination is assigned. Historical river use is not current crossing advice; river and tide conditions can submerge the stones.

legend.title: Hawise and the common
legend.label: Local folklore · undated
legend.text: In one local tale, a Norman lord's daughter wins freedom for a Welsh prisoner and claims common land by walking its boundary before sunset. Retellings disagree about names and relationships. This is a tradition associated with the area, not evidence for a dated event or the legal origin of the common.
legend.note: Some versions place the family in Candleston in the 12th century, although the surviving fortified house is later. The legend therefore sits beside the timeline rather than becoming a medieval milestone.

additionalLegends.title: The White Lady and the hidden gold
additionalLegends.label: Local folklore · undated, recorded in 1909
additionalLegends.text: In a tale printed by Marie Trevelyan, the White Lady guards gold beneath a stone in Ogmore Castle's tower. A man is permitted to take half, but later returns for the rest. The story says she punishes his greed and he falls ill. It is a cautionary tale, not archaeological evidence for hidden treasure.
additionalLegends.note: 1909 is the collection's publication date, not a date for a haunting. Trevelyan also records other White Lady traditions around Ewenny; this is the Ogmore Castle version on pages 200–201.
